title: Behaviour change & oral health education
blurb: Why telling isn't enough: COM-B, the stages of change, motivational interviewing, SMART goals and how to deliver oral health advice that sticks.
question: A patient has had the same oral hygiene advice at her last three visits and nothing has changed. She says, 'I know I should floss, I just never get round to it.' The dentist asks you to do some oral health education with her. How will you approach it differently this time?

teach.body: Most patients already know they should brush, floss and cut down on sugar. What's missing is turning knowledge into a habit. Repeating the same facts, or lecturing, rarely changes behaviour and can make patients defensive. DBOH recommends using behaviour change methods alongside oral hygiene instruction, and getting the patient to set their own goals. Your aim is to work with the patient, not talk at them.

children.sub: Skills and knowledge: can they do it?

teach.caption: If any one is missing, the behaviour won't happen. Find which one is the barrier and target that.

teach.caption: Pre-contemplation: not thinking of changing. Contemplation: 'I know I should…'. Relapse is normal; people often go round several times.

teach.body: Motivational interviewing is a guiding, collaborative style of conversation that helps patients find their own reasons to change. Instead of telling ('You must floss'), you ask ('What would make it easier to clean between your teeth?') and listen. You resist the urge to correct and lecture, roll with resistance rather than arguing, and encourage 'change talk', where the patient voices their own wish or plan to change. People believe what they hear themselves say.

teach.caption: The patient chooses the goal. One small, achievable change beats a list of five.

teach.h: Delivering oral health advice that sticks
items: Find out what the patient already knows, does and wants.
Give one clear message at a time, in plain words with no jargon.
Tell, show, do: explain, demonstrate on a model, then let them try with a mirror.
Check understanding with teach-back: 'Can you show me how you'll do that at home?'
Agree one small, SMART goal, chosen by the patient.
Give a brief written reminder, then review and praise progress next visit.

teach.body: Adapt your approach to the person. Use a professional interpreter for patients whose first language isn't English, rather than relying on family. Offer large print, easy-read or pictorial resources, speak clearly facing patients who lip-read, and involve carers or parents where appropriate. Be aware of anxiety, low literacy, cultural beliefs and different diets. For children, make it fun and involve the parent. Make Every Contact Count: brief, positive messages at every visit add up.

teach.text: More information is not better. A long lecture or a pile of leaflets overloads patients and they remember little. One clear message, checked with teach-back and backed by a small agreed goal, works far better.

items: Behaviour needs Capability, Opportunity and Motivation (COM-B).
Stages of change: pre-contemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance (relapse is normal).
Motivational interviewing guides rather than tells: OARS.
Patients set SMART goals: one small, specific change at a time.
One message, tell-show-do, teach-back, written reminder, review next visit.

summary: You can now explain why information alone rarely changes behaviour, use COM-B and the stages of change to understand where a patient is, apply motivational interviewing skills (OARS), help a patient set a SMART goal, and deliver oral health advice with one clear message, tell-show-do and teach-back, adapting it to the patient's needs.

A.q: A nervous patient says dental advice confuses them because they get too much at once. What is the best approach?
options: Give all the advice in one go
Give one clear message at a time
Use technical terms to be precise
A.why: One clear message at a time avoids overload and makes the advice easier to remember and act on.

whyNot.0: Giving everything at once causes the overload the patient describes.
whyNot.2: Jargon makes advice harder to understand.
whyNot.3: Rushing makes it harder for the patient to take in.

A.q: A patient nods during oral hygiene instruction but looks unsure. What should you do next?
options: Assume the nod means they've understood
Repeat it more slowly and loudly
Ask them to show or explain it back
Move on to the next topic
A.why: Teach-back, asking the patient to explain or demonstrate, checks they have really understood.

whyNot.3: Moving on leaves the confusion unresolved.

A.q: Which goal is the best example of a SMART goal for a patient?
options: Floss every single tooth three times daily
Floss the lower front teeth each night
A.why: It is specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and can be reviewed at the next visit.

whyNot.0: This is vague and can't be measured.
whyNot.1: Three times daily across every tooth is unrealistic to start with.
whyNot.2: 'Forever' is unrealistic and impossible to measure.

B.q: A patient says, 'I know I should floss, but I never get round to it.' Which stage of change are they in?
B.why: They recognise the need to change but haven't started, which is the contemplation stage.

whyNot.1: In pre-contemplation, people aren't thinking about changing at all.
whyNot.2: In action, the person is already doing the new behaviour.
whyNot.3: Maintenance means the new behaviour has been kept up over time.

B.q: Which approach is most effective for oral health education?
options: Cover as much as possible in one visit
Give the same advice to everyone
Hand over a leaflet instead of talking
B.why: A two-way discussion tailored to the patient, with understanding checked, is more effective than one-way information.

whyNot.0: Too much information at once is quickly forgotten.
whyNot.1: Advice works best when tailored to the individual.
whyNot.3: Leaflets support but don't replace discussion.

B.q: Which of these is an open question?
options: Is your toothbrush a powered one?
How do you clean your teeth?
B.why: An open question invites the patient to describe things in their own words rather than answer yes or no.

whyNot.0: This can be answered yes or no, so it's a closed question.
whyNot.1: This is a closed, yes-or-no question.
whyNot.2: This is a closed question with a one-word answer.

C.q: A patient says they forget brushing advice soon after appointments. What is the best support?
C.why: A short written reminder reinforces the key message after the appointment.

whyNot.1: Withholding advice doesn't help them remember.
whyNot.2: Technical terms make advice harder to remember.
whyNot.3: Costs don't address their oral hygiene.

C.q: A patient hasn't changed their brushing since the last visit. Which approach best supports change?
options: Repeat the same advice as before
Set several changes to make at once
C.why: One small, realistic goal that the patient agrees to is more likely to be achieved and build confidence.

whyNot.0: Repeating advice that hasn't worked is unlikely to work now.
whyNot.2: Several changes at once can overwhelm and lead to none being made.
whyNot.3: Blame makes patients defensive and less likely to change.

C.q: In the COM-B model, a patient who wants to clean interdentally but has no interdental brushes at home lacks which component?
C.why: Having the right aids available is part of opportunity, the physical and social factors that make a behaviour possible.

whyNot.0: Capability is about skills and knowledge.
whyNot.1: They want to do it, so motivation is present.
whyNot.3: Maintenance is a stage of change, not part of COM-B.

reteach.title: Coach, not referee
reteach.question: Think of a good sports coach. Do they shout the rules at players, or help them improve one skill at a time? What does that mean for oral health advice?

blocks.body: A referee points out what you did wrong. A coach asks what you're finding hard, shows you one technique, lets you try it, praises what goes well and sets one thing to practise before next week. That's exactly how good oral health education works. Ask, listen, demonstrate, let them try, check they've got it and agree one small goal together. Next visit, start by asking how it went.

blocks.text: 'Do you understand?' almost always gets a yes. Ask the patient to show you or explain it back instead.

explain.body: A behaviour needs Capability (skills, knowledge), Opportunity (time, place, the right aids) and Motivation (wanting to, habits). Find the missing piece.

rows.label: 'I don't know how to use floss'

explain.note: Capability gap: demonstrate. Opportunity gap: supply or suggest aids. Motivation gap: explore their reasons.

test.q: A patient wants to floss and has floss at home, but can't work out how to use it. Which COM-B component is missing?
test.why: Not knowing how to do the behaviour is a lack of capability, so a demonstration is what's needed.

whyNot.0: They want to floss, so motivation is present.
whyNot.1: They have the floss and the chance to use it.
whyNot.3: Contemplation is a stage of change, not part of COM-B.

explain.body: Pre-contemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance, with relapse a normal part of the cycle. Match your approach to the stage the patient is in.

test.q: A patient says, 'My gums are fine, I don't need to change anything.' Which stage are they in?
test.why: They aren't considering change at all, which is pre-contemplation.

whyNot.0: Preparation means they're planning to change soon.
whyNot.2: Action means they're already making the change.
whyNot.3: Maintenance means a change has already become a habit.

explain.body: A guiding style: open questions, affirmations, reflective listening and summarising (OARS). Avoid lecturing; help the patient voice their own reasons to change.

test.q: Which response is an example of reflective listening?
test.why: Reflective listening repeats back the meaning of what the patient said, showing you've understood.

whyNot.0: This is an instruction, not reflection.
whyNot.2: Handing over a leaflet isn't listening.

explain.body: Help the patient choose one Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-bound goal. Check understanding by asking them to explain or show it back.

test.q: Which part of a SMART goal is missing from 'I'll use interdental brushes on my back teeth every night'?
test.why: There's no time frame or review point, such as 'until my next visit in four weeks'.

whyNot.1: It names the aid and the area, so it's specific.
whyNot.3: One area each night is achievable.
